A multisite trial: the Online Credit Recovery Study

Source: vignettes/multisite-trial.Rmd
multisite-trial.Rmd

One trial can give several sets of site estimates, for example one for each outcome, each subset of sites, each choice of covariates or each effect measure. poolinfo’s diagnostics describe one such set together with its standard errors, so the same students can give different diagnostics. In this vignette we analyze the Online Credit Recovery Study as a whole, as Section 8 of Lee (2026) does. We take its two outcomes, its two subjects, a covariate-adjusted analysis and three first-stage analyses of passing, and for each outcome we say what we would do next. If the informativeness II, the mean reliability S‾\bar S, the dispersion HH, the logit variance VV or the concentration count JeffJ_{\mathrm{eff}} is new to you, vignette("poolinfo") defines them, with the passing outcome as its example.

library(poolinfo)

The trial and its site estimates

In the summers of 2018 and 2019, the study assigned students in Los Angeles high schools by lottery to one of two versions of their school’s summer course, an online course or the usual course directed by a teacher (Rickles et al. 2024; American Institutes for Research 2024). All of them had failed Algebra 1 or English 9 in their first year. A site is one school’s course in one subject, and the data set ocrs has a row for each site in which students were assigned to both versions. We count the sites in each subject and the schools, and summarize the sites’ sizes.

table(ocrs$subject)
#> 
#> Algebra 1 English 9 
#>        13        19
length(unique(ocrs$school))
#> [1] 24
summary(ocrs$n)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   24.00   39.75   49.00   54.28   64.50  104.00

Of the 32 sites, 13 are in Algebra 1 and 19 in English 9. They belong to 24 schools, so 8 schools have a site in each subject. A site has 24 to 104 students, and the median site has 49.

Within each site, the estimate is the coefficient of the treatment indicator in a least squares regression of the outcome on that indicator and the randomization blocks, with the HC2 standard error. This coefficient is a weighted average of the blocks’ differences between the two courses, with weights proportional to nkpk(1−pk)n_k p_k (1 - p_k), where nkn_k is the size of block kk and pkp_k the proportion of its students assigned to the online course. A block whose students all took the same course gets no weight. An average effect over all the site’s students would weight each block by its size nkn_k instead, and the two weightings differ in all 28 sites that have more than one block (Lee 2026, sec. 8 and Appendix G). Each estimate is therefore a block-adjusted contrast, which can differ from the effect averaged over the site’s students.

ocrs contains five sets of site estimates, each with its standard errors:

  • estimate, se: course passing, as the block-adjusted difference in the proportions passing.
  • estimate_adjusted, se_adjusted: the same regression with four baseline covariates added, the grade 8 state test score in the subject and the grade 9 GPA, each with an indicator of a missing value.
  • estimate_credits, se_credits: credits earned in the subject by the end of the fourth year of high school, from the same regression as estimate.
  • estimate_unadjusted, se_unadjusted: the difference in the proportions passing between the two courses, ignoring the blocks.
  • log_odds_ratio, se_log_odds_ratio: the log odds ratio of passing, from the same table of course by outcome as the unadjusted difference, so it ignores the blocks too.

?ocrs describes how each pair was computed from the study’s public-use file. If you start from student records of your own, you compute such estimates and standard errors site by site and then pass them to poolinfo.

Outcomes, subjects and covariates

We fit the posterior for passing in all 32 sites and in each subject, for adjusted passing and for credits. Each fit records the scale of its effects and the estimand at each site (scale_label and target_label), which the table at the end repeats, and compare_profiles() collects the fits.

rd <- "risk difference"
itt <- "the block-adjusted intention-to-treat contrast for course passing"
fit_passing <- function(data) {
  reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, site = site, data = data,
                        scale_label = rd, target_label = itt)
}
algebra <- ocrs$subject == "Algebra 1"
fits <- list(
  passing = fit_passing(ocrs),
  `passing, Algebra 1` = fit_passing(ocrs[algebra, ]),
  `passing, English 9` = fit_passing(ocrs[!algebra, ]),
  `passing, adjusted` = reliability_posterior(
    estimate_adjusted, se = se_adjusted, site = site, data = ocrs,
    scale_label = rd,
    target_label = "the covariate-adjusted contrast for course passing"
  ),
  credits = reliability_posterior(
    estimate_credits, se = se_credits, site = site, data = ocrs,
    scale_label = "credit",
    target_label = "the block-adjusted contrast for credits by year 4"
  )
)
comparison <- compare_profiles(.list = fits)
comparison
#> Comparison of 5 analyses
#> Intervals are central posterior intervals.
#> Each analysis is conditional on its own standard errors.
#> 
#>   analysis            J   informativeness I     mean reliability
#>   passing             32  0.671 [0.497, 0.812]  0.663
#>   passing, Algebra 1  13  0.629 [0.294, 0.865]  0.625
#>   passing, English 9  19  0.707 [0.493, 0.868]  0.698
#>   passing, adjusted   32  0.652 [0.474, 0.800]  0.644
#>   credits             32  0.318 [0.022, 0.597]  0.327
#> 
#>   analysis            dispersion H             concentration count J_eff
#>   passing             0.0253 [0.0185, 0.0289]  31.2
#>   passing, Algebra 1  0.0164 [0.0086, 0.0196]  12.7
#>   passing, English 9  0.0284 [0.0176, 0.0342]  18.5
#>   passing, adjusted   0.0279 [0.0205, 0.0317]  31.0
#>   credits             0.0285 [0.0031, 0.0376]  28.8

Of these analyses, the two outcomes differ most. For passing, the posterior mean of II is 0.67 (95% posterior interval 0.50 to 0.81), so a site with the geometric-mean standard error keeps about 67% of its own estimate. For credits, II is 0.32 (0.02 to 0.60), and such a site keeps only about 32% of its estimate. The posterior probability that II exceeds 1/2, the value at which the model would move such a site halfway toward the mean effect, is 0.97 for passing and 0.11 for credits, with 1/2 as a reference point only. Site by site, the reliabilities run from 0.42 to 0.84 for passing and from 0.11 to 0.51 for credits, and the concentration counts are 31.2 and 28.8 of 32. For passing the mean reliability is a little below II (0.663 against 0.671), and for credits a little above it (0.327 against 0.318). These are the directions that the leading term of S‾−I\bar S - I gives when II is above or below 1/2.

In the average site, assignment to the online course lowered the proportion passing by 13.0 percentage points (95% posterior interval 5.0 to 21.1). Its effect on the credits earned has a posterior mean of -0.1 credits (-1.9 to 1.6).

These diagnostics lead us to different next steps for the two outcomes. As Lee (2026) concludes, the passing profile supports a closer look at the effects of the individual sites, starting from the posterior means and intervals of site_table(). Ranking the sites would still call for its own measure of uncertainty, because the diagnostics describe the estimates as a whole. The credits profile gives a more uncertain basis for such an analysis, and for credits we would report the mean effect and the between-site standard deviation before turning to individual sites.

Adding the baseline covariates lowers II for passing from 0.671 to 0.652. Covariates that predict the outcome usually shrink the standard errors, which would raise II. Here, though, the HC2 standard errors grew in 20 of the 32 sites, and their geometric mean rose from 0.128 to 0.131. Meanwhile the posterior mean of στ\sigma_\tau fell a little, from 0.188 to 0.184. Each analysis is conditional on its own standard errors, so a first-stage choice that changes them changes the diagnostics too.

Each subject’s analysis describes its own set of sites and has its own between-site standard deviation. With 13 and 19 sites, their posterior intervals for II are wider than the pooled one: 0.29 to 0.87 for Algebra 1 and 0.49 to 0.87 for English 9. To analyze all 32 sites together while letting the two subjects have different mean effects, we put the subject in the mean model instead. Each site is then pulled toward the mean of its subject, and στ\sigma_\tau describes the variation around the two means.

by_subject <- reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, site = site,
                                    data = ocrs, mean_model = ~ subject)
by_subject
#> Reliability profile of 32 sites (posterior)
#> Model: estimate ~ N(effect, se^2), effect ~ N(x'beta, sigma_tau^2),
#>        sites independent
#> Prior: flat on the coefficients of the mean model and on sigma_tau
#> Summaries are conditional on the supplied standard errors.
#> Each site counts equally in the diagnostics, whatever its size.
#> 
#>                                mean     95% interval
#>   informativeness I            0.672    0.496    0.814
#>   mean reliability             0.664    0.497    0.804
#>   dispersion H                 0.0252   0.0183   0.0289
#>   concentration count J_eff    31.2     30.3     31.7     of 32
#>   logit variance V             0.237    (fixed by the standard errors)
#>   sigma_tau                    0.188    0.127    0.268
#>   coefficient (Intercept)      -0.0805  -0.209   0.0481
#>   coefficient subjectEnglish 9 -0.0827  -0.248   0.0821
#> 
#>   Pr(I > 0.5)                  0.973
#>   I at E(sigma_tau^2)          0.692

In this fit the English 9 sites’ mean effect is 8.3 percentage points below that of the Algebra 1 sites, with a 95% posterior interval for the difference from 24.8 points below to 8.2 points above. With στ\sigma_\tau at 0.188, as with a common mean, II is 0.672 against 0.671, so taking out the difference between the subjects leaves the variation between sites where it was.

Posteriors of the informativeness

Next we compare the posterior densities of II for the two outcomes. We keep the pair of fits in outcomes, which also gives the table at the end.

outcomes <- compare_profiles(passing = fits$passing, credits = fits$credits)
plot_functionals(outcomes)

The shaded 95% posterior intervals overlap only between 0.50 and 0.60. At the left edge the credits density rises without bound, and the plot cuts it off. This happens in every analysis under the flat prior, because the posterior density of στ\sigma_\tau is positive at 0 and, near 0, II grows like στ2\sigma_\tau^2. How much of it shows depends on how high the posterior of στ\sigma_\tau is at 0. For passing that height is about 10−910^{-9} of the posterior’s peak, so nothing is visible, but for credits it is 0.09 of the peak.

Dashed lines mark II at the posterior mean of στ2\sigma_\tau^2, 0.691 for passing and 0.353 for credits. Both lie right of the solid lines, the posterior means, because II is a concave function of στ2\sigma_\tau^2(Lee 2026, Proposition 3), and the gap is 0.020 for passing and 0.035 for credits.

The contrast and the effect measure

Reporting the effects in percentage points rather than proportions multiplies every estimate and standard error by 100. Under the flat prior the diagnostics stay the same, because στ\sigma_\tau grows by the same factor as the standard errors (Lee 2026, Appendix G); a proper prior would need its scale multiplied too. A different contrast or a different effect measure is another kind of change, since it alters the spread of the true effects and the standard errors in different ways. We compare three analyses of passing: the block-adjusted difference used so far, the unadjusted difference in the proportions passing, and the log odds ratio. Both of the last two come from the same table of course by outcome in each site, so the step between them changes the effect measure alone.

unadjusted <- reliability_posterior(estimate_unadjusted, se = se_unadjusted,
                                    data = ocrs)
log_odds <- reliability_posterior(log_odds_ratio, se = se_log_odds_ratio,
                                  data = ocrs)
scales <- compare_profiles(`difference, block-adjusted` = fits$passing,
                           `difference, unadjusted` = unadjusted,
                           `log odds ratio` = log_odds)
scales
#> Comparison of 3 analyses
#> Intervals are central posterior intervals.
#> Each analysis is conditional on its own standard errors.
#> 
#>   analysis                    J   informativeness I     mean reliability
#>   difference, block-adjusted  32  0.671 [0.497, 0.812]  0.663
#>   difference, unadjusted      32  0.632 [0.439, 0.790]  0.628
#>   log odds ratio              32  0.530 [0.253, 0.743]  0.530
#> 
#>   analysis                    dispersion H             concentration count J_eff
#>   difference, block-adjusted  0.0253 [0.0185, 0.0289]  31.2
#>   difference, unadjusted      0.0211 [0.0160, 0.0231]  31.2
#>   log odds ratio              0.0346 [0.0263, 0.0367]  30.2

Dropping the blocks lowers II from 0.671 to 0.632, and the log odds ratio lowers it again, to 0.530, with a posterior probability of 0.63 that II exceeds 1/2. Next we place the three analyses in the plane of II and VV, with contours of the leading term of the dispersion, I(1−I)V/2I(1 - I)V/2.

plot(scales, type = "plane")

The log odds ratio lies above the two differences in the plane, at V=0.31V = 0.31 against 0.19 for the unadjusted difference and 0.24 for the block-adjusted one. Its sampling variance grows as a site’s passing proportions approach 0 or 1, whereas a difference’s is largest when they are near 1/2, so the two measures spread the same sites’ standard errors differently. Both differences lie between the contours at 0.02 and 0.03, and the log odds ratio between 0.03 and 0.04, in line with their dispersions of 0.025, 0.021 and 0.035. In a report we would name both the contrast and the effect measure, as the labels of the fits for the outcomes do.

Schools with two sites

Each of the 8 schools with a site in each subject contributes two estimates, and some of its students appear in both, while the model treats all 32 sites as independent. Each site also counts once in the diagnostics, whatever its size, so these schools count twice. To see how much this matters, we keep one site of each such school, in all 28=2562^{8} = 256 ways, and refit both outcomes to each set of 24 sites.

paired <- as.integer(names(which(table(ocrs$school) == 2)))
choices <- expand.grid(rep(list(c("Algebra 1", "English 9")), length(paired)))
I_of <- function(fit) subset(profile_summary(fit), quantity == "I")$mean
I_subsets <- t(apply(choices, 1, function(subject) {
  keep <- !(ocrs$school %in% paired) |
    paste(ocrs$school, ocrs$subject) %in% paste(paired, subject)
  sites <- ocrs[keep, ]
  c(passing = I_of(reliability_posterior(estimate, se = se, data = sites)),
    credits = I_of(reliability_posterior(estimate_credits, se = se_credits,
                                         data = sites)))
}))
apply(I_subsets, 2, range)
#>        passing   credits
#> [1,] 0.6120245 0.1159935
#> [2,] 0.7480950 0.4207495

Across the 256 sets of 24 sites, the posterior mean of II runs from 0.612 to 0.748 for passing and from 0.116 to 0.421 for credits, against 0.671 and 0.318 with all 32 sites. Passing stays above 1/2 and credits below it in every set, so the contrast between the outcomes survives whichever site of a paired school we keep. These refits vary the set of sites. Allowing for the students who appear in both of a school’s sites would take a model with the covariance between the school’s two estimates, which the working model leaves out (Lee 2026, sec. 9).

A table for the report

report_table() lays out a comparison in the format of Table 5 of Lee (2026) and adds a note for the readers of the report. We make the table for the two outcomes.

cat(report_table(outcomes, format = "markdown"))
Analysis J I [95% interval] Mean reliability H [95% interval] J_eff Pr(I > 0.5)
passing 32 .67 [.50, .81] .66 .025 [.019, .029] 31.2 .97
credits 32 .32 [.02, .60] .33 .028 [.003, .038] 28.8 .11

Note. Each estimate is modeled as normal around its site’s effect with a known sampling variance, and the site effects as independent and normal across sites. Flat priors on the mean and the between-site standard deviation. Scales of the effects: risk difference (passing); credit (credits). Estimands at each site: the block-adjusted intention-to-treat contrast for course passing (passing); the block-adjusted contrast for credits by year 4 (credits). Summaries are conditional on the supplied standard errors, and each site counts equally in the diagnostics, whatever its size.

The note under the table carries the scale and the estimand that we set for each outcome. Called with comparison, report_table() makes the table for all five analyses, and with format = "latex" it writes the table as LaTeX code with the rules of the booktabs package.
